event.title: When We Bridge: Indigenous Peoples’ Guardianship, Knowledge, and Global Impact
event.description:
Join us for the inaugural Center for Just Environmental Futures Distinguished Lecture
Featuring - ‘Aulani Wilhelm, CEO of Nia Tero

Reception following program from 6:00-6:30pm.

About our speaker: ‘Aulani Wilhelm is Kanaka ‘Ōiwi (Native Hawaiian), born and raised in Hawaiʻi. ʻAulani is the Chief Executive Officer at Nia Tero, an organization focused solely on Indigenous guardianship and the role Indigenous Peoples have played and can continue to play—in protecting lands, waters, and ocean areas as antidotes to the global climate crisis and biodiversity loss. She joined Nia Tero in October 2023 after serving as the Assistant Director for Ocean Conservation, Climate and Equity at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. ‘Aulani previously served as the Senior Vice President for Oceans at Conservation International where she co-led the Blue Nature Alliance, a global partnership to catalyze the conservation of 18 million km2 of ocean. ‘Aulani led the establishment of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument and World Heritage Site and co-founded Big Ocean, a network of the world’s largest marine managed areas. Prior, she was director of ocean initiatives for NOAA’s Office of Marine Sanctuaries, and a social innovation fellow at Stanford University. ‘Aulani is a Mellon Distinguished Scholar at Arizona State University’s Center for Imagination at the Borderlands. She holds a MS degree from Stanford University and a BA degree from the University of Southern California.

About the Center for Just Environmental Futures: The Stanford Center for Just Environmental Futures (Futures Center) advances rigorous scholarship, education, and collaboration at the intersection of justice and sustainability. The Center brings together faculty, researchers, students, and community partners to address the intertwined challenges of environmental degradation, climate change, and inequality—recognizing that environmental crises exacerbate inequities, inequities fuel environmental crises, and enduring solutions must strengthen both human dignity and ecological resilience.

Our Co-Sponsors: Center for Just Environmental Futures, Center for Human and Planetary Health, Native American Studies, and Native American Cultural Center

event.title: BOOK LAUNCH: Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 80, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
The Department of African and African American Studies (DAAAS) in collaboration with the Center for South Asia (CSA) cordially invite the Stanford Community for a special book launch!

We are excited to celebrate the publication of a new book by our visiting postdoctoral scholar, Danny Shanhan, Ph.D titled, Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland.

This book is the first substantial study of emergency law's relationship to literature in either the Northern Irish or the Kashmiri conflict and develops an original legal history that links these laws to a shared British colonial root. Engaging a wide range of fiction, poetry and film, from canonical poets Seamus Heaney and Agha Shahid Ali to contemporary works by Anna Burns, Mirza Waheed, and Bollywood filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj, the book examines the literary response to the suspension of normative legal rights such as habeas corpus, the right to silence and even, in Kashmir, the right to life. By bringing these literary cultures together for the first time, it develops a literary and legal history that reveals common roots in colonial-era jurisprudence. The book re-situates these corpora, often isolated in scholarly work, as important parts of the global, material legacies of colonialism.

Join us for an evening of conversation, community and celebration and Danny shares his work. This will be followed by a discussion and Q&A with Roanne Kantor, Assistant Professor of English.

Refreshments will be provided.

event.title: Open Wide the Doors: The Prison Memoirs of Mahvash Sabet
event.ticket_cost: Free and open to the public. Register for Zoom link.
event.description:
In 2018, during her brief respite of freedom between two decade-long prison sentences, Mahvash Sabet asked Bahiyyih Nakhjavani and Azita Mottahedeh to work on her memoirs and make a book that could convey her story in English. They set to work, with Mottahedeh translating the Persian original, word for word, and Nakhjavani attempting to structure a narrative from the more than 750 pages of a harrowing and uplifting testimony which Sabet smuggled out of prison over the years.

“In this discussion, we will explore the decisions involved and the methods followed in the course of creating this book, as well as the distinctive characteristics of Mahvash Sabet's style, tone and intent, which we hope have survived the translation.  We will share the ways in which this prison memoir may be different from others and at the same time how it seems to bear witness to the many which might never be written.  Above all we will try to share Mahvash’s extraordinary capacity to transform despair into hope, confinement into freedom, and estrangement and isolation into a boundless compassion towards others.”

Bahiyyih Nakhjavani was born in Iran, raised in Uganda, and educated in the UK and the US. She received her preliminary degrees in English Literature from the University of York in the UK, and completed her doctorate at UMass, Amherst, in the US, as well as being awarded an honorary doctorate by the University of Liège in Belgium. In addition to teaching literature and creative writing over four decades, she is the author of several novels about Iran and Iranians, including The Saddlebag, Paper, The Woman Who Read Too Much, and Us&Them, published by Bloomsbury and Stanford University Press and translated into a dozen other languages. She has also written essays and articles about the Bahá’í Faith published by George Ronald, UK. Most recently, she has been adapting Persian poetry into English and has translated and edited the memoirs of the prisoner of conscience, Mahvash Sabet, entitled Open Wide The Doors, published by Oneworld in the UK in 2026. Bahiyyih Nakhjavani currently lives in France and narrates audio recordings in English.

Azita Mottahedeh was born in Iran and educated in the UK where she attended the universities of Canterbury and Reading at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. As a translator from Persian to English, she has specialised in works about the Bahá’í Faith for more than thirty years.

Her translations include articles and talks, memoirs and poetry, as well as books of philosophy, history and theology, including 175 Years of Persecution: A History of the Bábís and Bahá’ís of Iran by Dr F. Vahman. Other works she has translated include The Life of Anís Zunúzí by R. Mehrabkhani, The Kingdom of Existence by Dr Ali-Murád Dávúdí, and Volumes I & II of Radio Talks by H. Fatheazam. Several of her translations are in the process of publication. She currently lives in Spain.

This event is made possible by a generous gift from the Taslimi Foundation, establishing a new endowment at Stanford Iranian Studies for the study of the Baha’i Faith in Iran.

event.title: Book Talk: Changing Gender
event.description:
Join Stryker as she discusses her latest book, Changing Gender, where she invites readers to ride along on her lifelong quest to uncover what gender means and does. She traces the gender concept’s roots in grammar and tells the story of how it transformed into a battleground of the culture wars. From the origins of “Yankee Doodle” to acid trips in Joshua Tree National Park, from 19th-century phrenology to present-day anti-trans conspiracy theorists, Stryker finds surprising places to tune in to the origins, idiosyncrasies, and generative possibilities of the gender concept. Along the way, she weaves stories drawn from her lifetime as a pathbreaking historian, filmmaker, activist, and founding figure of transgender studies.

Poignant and deeply researched, lyrical and authoritative, Changing Gender is a book for our fraught time, exposing limiting assumptions about gender across the political spectrum and imagining what life might look like if some of those limitations were lifted. Ultimately, Stryker argues, to change gender is to change what it means to be human – and to change reality itself.

RSVP here

About the Speaker:

Susan Stryker is professor emerita of gender and women’s studies at the University of Arizona and currently serves as distinguished visitor at Stanford’s Clayman Institute for Gender Research. Since retiring, Stryker has served as presidential fellow and visiting professor of gender, women’s, and sexuality studies at Yale University; Barbara Lee Distinguished Chair in Women’s Leadership, Mills College; and Marta Sutton Weeks External Faculty Fellow, Stanford University Humanities Institute. She is the author of three editions of Transgender History, co-editor of the two-volume Transgender Studies Reader and The Transgender Studies Reader Remix, as well as co-director of the Emmy-winning documentary film Screaming Queens: The Riot at Compton’s Cafeteria.

event.title: DAAAS Fall Faculty Research Seminar(s)
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 80, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Please join DAAAS for the Fall Quarter Faculty Research Seminars on first thursdays from 12-1.30pm.

The speaker line-up:

October 8:  Power, Historiography, Photography--Professor Joshua Cohen, Associate Professor of Art and Art History and, by courtesy, of African and African American Studies.

Description: The place of photography in the historiography of African modernism raises significant questions for the discipline of art history and for African and postcolonial studies more broadly. Independence-era portraits and nightlife scenes by the Malian photographers Seydou Keita and Malick Sidibé in Bamako, and by the Angolan-born photographer Jean Depara in Léopoldville/Kinshasa, among others, are commonly accorded a documentary authority that anchors relationships between aesthetics and politics, modern self-fashioning and decolonization. Yet to recall anthropologist Simon Ottenberg’s 1993 observation that African art studies aimed mostly “to show the positive and cohesive view of African life in the face of so many negative stereotypes in the West” is to ask how much the field’s aesthetic and political parameters have really changed since that time. Even when independence-era photos are read in political terms, they tend to imply a somewhat selective vision of the political gleaned through the confidence and style of individual portrait subjects and image-makers. How do such readings mesh with the much more complicated histories of African decolonization and the Cold War that are by now well documented? And what do such readings suggest about the current role of art history, the art museum, and the humanities within global power structures and information ecosystems?

Joshua I. Cohen is a historian of modern art specializing in postcolonial, African/diaspora, and global Cold War studies. His research and teaching explore modernist practices and discourses spanning francophone West Africa, southern Africa, Europe, the Caribbean, and the United States

November 12 :  Empathy in Black Studies--Dr.Timothy Pantoja, Mellon Fellow of the Humanities at Stanford University and a Lecturer in the Department of African and African American Studies.

Description: This talk traces the productive tensions between empathy as a moral idea and empathy as an aesthetic practice in Black Studies. In particular, I analyze how Zora Neale Hurston’s ideas on embodied spectatorship forecasts both the critique of empathy as a moral shortcut and the current turns towards the haptic in black aesthetics. While Hurston is celebrated as an anthropologist, novelist, and choreographer her aesthetic insights on participatory perception, what she calls “watching”, remain under-appreciated. Therefore, this talk examines the ways Hurston improvised upon aesthetic ideas across the Enlightenment to contemporary ideas on kinesthesia to theorize the reflective dimensions of everyday practices of black expressivity.

Dr. Pantoja's research explores the ways Black and Caribbean literature and art theorize reflection, doubt, and what it means to participate with the objects that mediate our encounters with each other and a shareable world. His current book project, Scenes of Reflection: Compelling Insinuations, Empathy, and Absorption, analyzes portrayals of reflection in black modernist art and literature alongside the aesthetic evolutions of empathy as a mode of perception

December 10: Law as Epistemology: Religion, Narrative and Nomos in Maryse Condé’s historical fiction-Dr. Danny Shanadan, is a visiting postdoctoral fellow working collaboratively between Stanford University and University College Cork, Ireland.

Description:Following Subaltern Studies’ contention that subaltern ontologies and epistemologies are fundamentally religious, the talk argues that fictional work conceptualizes religion as a form through which the subjectivities and political goals of the historically marginalized are often expressed. It will address the shifting roles of law and religion in the lives of the marginalized through the Islamization of West Africa in Maryse Condé’s Segu, the transformation of Hindu peasant piety into Gandhian nationalist fervor in Raja Rao’s Kanthapura and in the burgeoning genre of convent murder-mystery in Ireland. I argue that fictional work intervenes on historical accounts of religious practice by depicting the social dynamism of belief systems. In historical fiction, religious hermeneutics become simultaneously law-defending and law-positing—both deeply intertwined with hegemonic legal narratives and at the same time a potentially liberatory, alternative epistemology.  

Dr. Shanadan completed his PhD at the University of Cambridge in 2024 and completed an Irish Research Council postdoctoral fellowship at University College Cork in 2025. His first monograph, ‘Literature and Emergency Law in Kashmir and Northern Ireland: Disturbed Areas’ combines law and literature studies with legal history to reveal the common British colonial roots of modern emergency laws used in the conflicts in Kashmir and Northern Ireland. This publication will be launched on wed. Nov. 11 2026 in building 80.

Location: Building 80 (Main Quad), Room 114

Lunch will be provided.

event.title: Earth System Science Seminar Series: Dr. Jenan Kharbush
event.description:
EARTH SYSTEM SCIENCE
SEMINAR SERIES

November 12, 2026
12:00 - 1:00 PM
Y2E2, Room 299


Jenan Kharbush, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor
University of Michigan

 

“A moving nitrogen target: How nitrogen availability and speciation shape the ecology of Microcystis-dominated cyanobacterial blooms” 


Abstract
In cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) dominated by the non-diazotrophic cyanobacterium Microcystis, nitrogen availability is critical for production of the nitrogen-rich toxin microcystin, and may also play a role in shaping Microcystis strain composition and relative abundance of toxic and non-toxic strains. During the annual CyanoHAB in Western Lake Erie, the dominant nitrogen pools shift between inorganic and organic forms as the bloom progresses. At the same time, Microcystis strain composition and the heterotrophic bacterial communities associated with Microcystis colonies also change. Recent metagenomics and culture-based work suggests that some of these heterotrophs participate in nitrogen acquisition and cycling processes with Microcystis. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to understand the influence of nitrogen availability and speciation on Microcystis bloom ecology using nano-secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS), complemented by shotgun metagenomic and transcriptomic community data. Our results suggest that Microcystis maintains a broad capacity to assimilate multiple nitrogen substrates across all bloom phases, effectively remaining primed to exploit shifting nitrogen pools regardless of their ambient concentrations. This flexibility may help sustain Microcystis dominance under changing bloom conditions.

 

Biography
I am an Assistant Professor in the Earth and Environmental Sciences Department at the University of Michigan. event.description:
Speaker: Shang-Ping Xie
Distinguished Professor of Climate Science, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego

More information forthcoming

Abstract: 

As early as March, the ECMWF and other climate forecast centers predicted a strong El Niño event for 2026—a forecast that has largely materialized, with Eastern Pacific sea surface temperature anomalies breaking century-long records. This super El Niño shares a distinctive two-part evolution common to the extreme El Niño events of 1982, 1997, and 2015. Specifically, the classic basin-scale El Niño driven by a deepened thermocline is preceded by a springtime (February–May) "booster" linked to the slow eastward expansion of the western Pacific warm pool coupled with westerly wind anomalies. The seminar presents real-time observations in relation to key El Niño precursors in the literature.

In 2025, Americans spent more than 400 billion hours inside work organizations. Nir Halevy's argument is that what happens in those hours, how people are ranked, rewarded, promoted, and treated, is one of the most consequential ways corporations shape society, even when it never reaches the headlines. event.title: Jeanet Sinding Bentzen — Risky Business? Religiosity and Risk-Taking in Full-Population Danish Data
event.description:
Why do individuals differ so persistently in their willingness to take economic risks? This paper investigates whether religiosity, particularly the intensity of religious belief, and helps explain this variation. The research considers two competing theoretical predictions: religious teachings discourage immoral and unlawful behavior, while the religious coping literature suggests that belief in a benevolent God reduces background anxiety and effectively provides psychological insurance. Using Danish administrative data covering the full population over three decades, together with a novel naming-based measure of individual religiosity, the paper finds that more religious individuals are significantly more likely to be self-employed and to hold a larger share of their assets in stocks. These effects are economically meaningful, corresponding to roughly a quarter of the wealth effect on economic risk-taking. The findings also remain significant when comparing individuals within sibling groups, which absorbs family-level confounders. The research further finds that these same individuals are less likely to be charged with a criminal offence. This pattern of opposite effects across different types of risk is consistent with the idea that religiosity reduces perceived background risk through a psychological insurance channel, while simultaneously increasing the perceived cost of behaviours condemned by religious teachings. Overall, the paper suggests that religiosity helps explain a portion of the large and persistent individual differences in risk-taking behavior.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Jeanet Sinding Bentzen is a Professor of Economics at the University of Copenhagen, where she also leads the department's PhD program. She is a Research Affiliate at the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) and the Centre for Competitive Advantage in the Global Economy (CAGE), Associate Editor at The Economic Journal, and Executive Director of the Association for the Study of Religion, Economics, and Culture (ASREC).

Her research lies in the economics of religion field. Using natural experiments and large-scale data, she studies why religiosity differs across the globe and how it shapes societies. Her work shows that crises such as earthquakes and the COVID-19 pandemic raise religiosity, that the divide between devout and secular people is the widest cultural gap on Earth, and that religiosity affects science, democracy, productivity, and conservative attitudes. She has published in The Economic Journal, the American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, the Journal of Development Economics, and Nature Communications, and her findings have been covered by The Economist, The Wall Street Journal, and Freakonomics Radio.

event.title: Pattern Magic: 3D Rendering of Archival Sewing Patterns
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 160, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Clothing is a complex and sensitive record of history—evincing the interplay of culture, technology, and artistry. At the same time, textile goods are notoriously difficult to conserve and display; in this context, paper sewing patterns provide a valuable record of historical clothing and methods of clothing manufacture. Our project, “Pattern Magic,” aims to dramatically improve the quantity and quality of historical garments available for research and creative use by (1) creating a database of 3D garments reconstructed from 60K historical patterns (earliest from the 1850s) available in the Commercial Pattern Archive (held at the University of Rhode Island) and (2) developing user-friendly tools which allow individuals and libraries to use our methods to contribute to this or other databases.

About the Speakers

Noah Toyonaga is a physicist and artist. They earned their PhD in physics from Harvard University in May 2025. They are drawn to the mysteries and delights of the everyday, which they explore, and try to explain, through theory, computation, and experiment—driven by geometric intuition.  As a Stanford Science Fellow (2025-2028), Noah studies the geometry and mechanics of soft membranes decorated by seams, a geometric motif that underlies the patterns drafted by a tailor and the microscale mechanisms evolved by single-celled organisms alike.

Conlan Olson is a PhD student in computer science at Columbia University advised by Professors Toni Pitassi and Rich Zemel. They study social aspects of computation, focusing on algorithmic fairness, privacy, and applications of computational methods to the humanities. Their background is in math, theoretical computer science, and education.

event.title: Environmental Behavioral Sciences Seminar with Leah Stokes
event.description:
The Political Economics of Sustainability Conference

https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/events/political-economics-sustainability

Location: Vidalakis Dining Hall

 

Electoral Returns from Climate Policy: The Effect of the Inflation Reduction Act’s Manufacturing Investments

Policy feedback theory predicts concentrated, visible benefits can generate electoral rewards for the party that enacted them. But climate policy that centers costs often produces electoral backlash. Can climate policy centered on benefits generate positive feedback? The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 used manufacturing tax credits to build a domestic clean energy supply chain, in theory boosting Democratic vote share where factories were built. We test this using a panel of 435 congressional districts across five presidential elections (2008–2024) merged with an original dataset of 523 clean energy manufacturing facilities. Two-way fixed-effects estimators identify a gain of approximately 1.5 percentage points in 2024 Democratic presidential vote share in districts receiving a facility. Effects are positive and significant at every level of treatment intensity: linear specifications imply approximately 0.4 percentage points per additional manufacturing facility, and larger dollar investments are associated with larger electoral gains. Climate policy centered on benefits can avoid backlash and provide electoral returns.

Bio

Leah C. Stokes is the Anton Vonk Associate Professor of Environmental Politics at UC Santa Barbara and the author of The Carbon Wave: A Story of Democracy, Parenthood, and the Race to Protect Our Planet. She has championed climate policy in the United States at all levels of government and was selected for Time Magazine’s Time100 Next list and Business Insider’s top 30 global climate leaders. Trained at MIT, Columbia, and the University of Toronto, Stokes has been published in top scholarly journals, as well as The New York Times, Washington Post, and other popular media outlets. A recipient of a Harvard University Radcliffe Fellowship, she is also the author of the award-winning Short Circuiting Policy, which was listed as one of the top five climate books in 2020 by The New York Times. She is also a co-host of the climate podcast “A Matter of Degrees.”.

event.title: Delivering Humanitarian Aid in a Contested World
event.description:
Join us for a two-part panel discussion with IsraAID and partners exploring the future of humanitarian assistance in an increasingly contested and conflict-ridden world. The first panel will examine how aid organizations deliver relief when access, neutrality, and safety are absent or precarious, drawing on IsraAID's experience responding to crises across the globe. The second panel will turn to the Middle East, focusing on the promise and practical challenges of Arab-Israeli cooperation in delivering humanitarian assistance to communities in need around the region.

AGENDA
3:30 - 4:00 PM: GATHERING AND REGISTRATION

4:00 - 4:10 PM: INTRODUCTION

Speaker: Larry Diamond (Mosbacher Senior Fellow in Global Democracy, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, Stanford University)

4:10 - 4:50 PM: PANEL ONE — Delivering Humanitarian Assistance in 2026: Challenges and Opportunities

  • Sonali Korde (Senior Advisor, All Hands and Hearts)
  • Raphael Marcus (Deputy CEO, IsraAID)

Moderator: David Cornfield (Anne T. and Robert M. Bass Professor of Pediatric Pulmonary Medicine, Stanford University)

4:55 - 6:00 PM: PANEL TWO — Lessons from the Middle East: Arab-Israeli Cooperation in Humanitarian Aid

  • Dr. Yaroup Ajlouni (President, Jordan Health Aid Society International)
  • Diana Shehade-Nama (Director of Fundraising, Marketing and Communications, Rozana–Health Diplomacy)
  • Yotam Polizer (Global CEO, IsraAID)
  • Dr. Khaula Sawah (President, Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations-USA)

Moderator: Paul Wise (Richard E. Behrman Professor of Child Health and Society, Stanford University)

6:00 - 6:30 PM: Please join us for a light reception in the Coit D. Blacker Lobby of Encina Hall.


ABOUT IsraAID

Founded in 2001 as a coalition of Israeli organizations working in disaster relief and international development, IsraAID has grown into an independent NGO and the largest humanitarian aid organization in Israel. From earthquakes and hurricanes to epidemics and forced displacement, IsraAID has been at the forefront of responding to major humanitarian crises around the globe. They have worked in more than 60 countries and at any one time have around 300 staff members worldwide.

About the Speakers

Dr. Yaroup Ajlouni is a physician and humanitarian leader with more than 20 years of experience in emergency response, health systems, and regional cooperation across the Middle East and North Africa, and currently serves as President of Jordan Health Aid Society International. His work spans humanitarian diplomacy, cross-border partnerships, and locally led response models, with emergency and development programs in Jordan, Gaza, Syria, Yemen, and Sudan.

 

A physician scientist, Dr. David Cornfield is actively engaged in clinical medicine, teaching and research. In clinical arena, Dr. Cornfield is a Pediatrician with an active practice in both Pediatric Pulmonary Medicine and Pediatric Critical Care Medicine. In the research arena, Dr. Cornfield's lab addresses several large thematic issues. There is an active translational research component.

 

Larry Diamond is the William L. Clayton Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, the Mosbacher Senior Fellow in Global Democracy at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies (FSI), a Bass University Fellow in Undergraduate Education, and a professor by courtesy of Political Science and Sociology at Stanford University. At the Hoover Institution, he co-leads the Project on Taiwan in the Indo-Pacific Region. At FSI, he is among the core faculty of the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL), which he directed for six and a half years. He is the Faculty Chair of CDDRL's Jan Koum Israel Studies Program and is a member of the Program on Arab Reform and Development. He also co-leads the Global Digital Policy Incubator, based at FSI’s Cyber Policy Center. 

 

Sonali Korde is a Senior Advisor at All Hands and Hearts and the MD Anderson Visiting Fellow at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, specializing in humanitarian affairs, international development, global health, and foreign policy. She previously served as Assistant to the Administrator leading USAID's Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, and on the National Security Council staff as Director of Global Health and Development.

 

Raphael Marcus is the Deputy CEO of IsraAID, with more than 15 years of humanitarian leadership across fragile and conflict-affected contexts. He previously served as Chief Programs Officer at HIAS, overseeing operations across 25 country offices and creating the agency's Emergency Response Department, and before that led international operations for the German medical relief organization Humedica, directing responses to Typhoon Haiyan, the Ebola outbreak in Liberia, and the Nepal earthquake.

 

Yotam Polizer is the Global CEO of IsraAID, Israel's largest humanitarian NGO, currently active in 15 countries with a 25-year record of responding to crises in over 65 — from the 2011 Japan tsunami to the post-October 7th recovery effort in Israel, and today the earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia and the flash floods in Nepal. He personally directed the 2021 evacuation of more than 200 at-risk Afghans fleeing the Taliban, and is the 2023 recipient of the Charles Bronfman Prize.

 

Dr. Khaula Sawah is President of the Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations-USA (UOSSM USA), which she co-founded, and has devoted most of her time since 2011 to medical relief missions for Syrians affected by the crisis in Syria and Turkey. As UOSSM's first Executive Director in Turkey she directed medical operations inside Syria and supervised the establishment of Bab Al-Hawa Hospital, now the major emergency and specialty referral hospital in northern Syria.

 

Diana Shehade-Nama is Director of Fundraising, Marketing and Communications at Rozana, which she joined in 2019, spending her first years designing and coordinating the organization's cross-border health initiatives with institutional partners and healthcare professionals across Israel and Palestine before taking on fundraising and strategic communications. Her commitment to Israeli–Palestinian engagement also includes teaching at the Hand in Hand bilingual school for Jewish-Arab education in Jerusalem and teaching Palestinian Anglophone literature at Tel Aviv University.

 

Dr. Paul Wise is a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has been working as the Juvenile Care Monitor for the U.S. Federal Court overseeing the treatment of migrant children in U.S. border detention facilities. Wise’s most recent U.S.-focused work has addressed disparities in birth outcomes, regionalized specialty care for children, and Medicaid. His international work has focused on women’s and child health in violent and politically complex environments, including Ukraine, Gaza, Central America, Venezuela, and children in detention on the U.S.-Mexico border. Wise is the Richard E. Behrman Professor of Child Health and Society and Professor of Pediatrics, Division of Neonatology and Developmental Medicine, and Health Policy at Stanford University. He is also co-director of the Stanford Center for Prematurity Research and a Senior Fellow at both the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law and the Center for International Security and Cooperation, within the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, Stanford University.

Overview

The holiday season can bring a particular kind of pressure for families caring for a child with medical complexity or navigating life after loss — from well-meaning relatives who don't understand care routines to social obligations that feel impossible to meet. This session brings together a panel of parents, some currently caregiving and some bereaved, to talk honestly about what it looks like to protect your time, energy, and peace during this time of year. Panelists will share how they've learned to say no, to ask for the support they actually need, and to hold firm boundaries with extended family, friends, and even well-intentioned strangers. The conversation will also explore the added layer bereaved parents carry — navigating traditions, invitations, and other people's expectations of grief — while still honoring their own family's story. event.description:

Learn how the challenges of decommissioning Fukushima Daiichi brought together research expertise in Japan and led to the founding of Ookuma Diamond Device, followed by its journey toward commercialization and manufacturing. event.title: Making Letters: Typography Across Hand, Screen, and Loom
event.description:
RSVP Link: HTTPS://TINYURL.COM/STSAMY26

How do the tools used to create letterforms shape the way those forms are imagined, constructed, and understood? In this presentation, graphic designer, educator, type designer, and fiber artist Amy Copeland traces her evolving relationship with typography across analog, digital, and textile practices. Beginning with hand-lettered high school book covers and the construction of letterforms with gouache and a ruling pen in college, she follows this trajectory through professional art direction and digital typesetting, original typeface design, and her recent project of weaving the alphabet.

Through this practice-based account, Copeland considers how typographic knowledge moves between technologies and materials. Digital tools make letterforms reproducible, scalable, and precisely adjustable; weaving translates those same forms into physical structures governed by warp, weft, tension, sequence, and touch. These material constraints do more than alter the appearance of a letter—they influence how it is conceived and constructed.Rather than treating analog and digital processes as opposites, Copeland explores the productive exchange between them. Her work demonstrates how knowledge gained through one form of making can migrate into another, revealing letters not as fixed symbols but as adaptable structures shaped by tools, materials, and embodied experience.

----------

Amy Copeland loves to make things. A graphic designer and educator for more than 30 years, she brings her interest in typography and letterforms to her weaving practice. She recently completed a woven alphabet and also creates tapestries and rugs using geometric shapes and patterns. Her work has been exhibited at Worthington Yards in Cleveland, Lakeland Community College, Cyrus Gallery, Malone College Art Gallery, and the McDonough Museum of Art at Youngstown State University.

Copeland is an Assistant Professor of Graphic + Interactive Design at Youngstown State University. She holds a BS in Graphic Design from the University of Cincinnati, an MFA in Visual Communication Design, and an MS in User Experience Design from Kent State University. She recently earned a postgraduate certificate in type design through the Type West program at Letterform Archive.

event.title: Eitner Lecture with M. D. Usher, "Journey to the West: Buddhists in Ancient Alexandria"
event.description:
Reception: Stanford Archaeology Center (500-106). Appetizers and drinks provided from 5:00 p.m. to 5:30 p.m.

Talk description:  The recent discovery of a Buddha statue in Berenike---the first West of Afghanistan---confirms the presence of Buddhists in Hellenistic Egypt. This talk argues that the Therapeutae, a monastic community of men and women described by Philo of Alexandria in On the Contemplative Life---long thought to be Jewish---were actually Buddhist.

Short bio: M. D. Usher is the Lyman-Roberts Professor Classical Languages and Literature at the University of Vermont. He teaches and writes on topics related to the environment, agriculture, traditional crafts, sustainability, utopian thinking, ancient philosophy, and oral art forms. He has just completed a biography of Plotinus for Princeton.

The Lorenz Eitner Lectures on Classical Art and Culture publicize classics and classical scholarship to a wider public. The series has been endowed by Peter and Lindsay Joost, great friends and benefactors of Stanford Classics, in honor of the late Lorenz Eitner, director of Stanford’s art museum, now known as the Cantor Center, in the 1960s-80s. He also chaired what was then the Department of Art and Architecture and was a distinguished expert of French Romantic painting, and the author of a dozen books on art and art history. In naming these annual lectures after him, we honor the memory of a renowned scholar, teacher and writer who oversaw the expansion of our art museum to a leading regional art collection.

This event is also sponsored by the Stanford Archaeology Center.

This talk will not be available on zoom and will not be recorded.

event.title: What is a Public Intellectual Today: Alexis Madrigal
event.description:
Please join us for the autumn event of the Stanford Public Humanities flagship speaker series, What Is a Public Intellectual Today, which will feature journalist Alexis Madrigal. He will be in conversation with Adrian Daub on craft, career, and culture in the Bay Area and beyond. Book signing and selling to follow for both authors. 

Please RSVP at this link to attend the event. 

Alexis Madrigal is an acclaimed multimedia journalist in Oakland, CA. He is the co-host of KQED’s current affairs show Forum, creator of the 8-part podcast Containers, author of the newsletter The Oakland Garden Club, and a contributing writer at The Atlantic, where he co-founded The COVID Tracking Project. His book The Pacific Circuit explores how a logistical revolution that began in Oakland has reshaped American cities. He is the proprietor of Local Economy, a community space in Oakland, and has been a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley’s School of Information and the Center for Science, Technology, Medicine & Society. 

Adrian Daub is J.E. Wallace Sterling Professor in the Humanities at Stanford University, where he serves as the Faculty Director of the Clayman Institute for Gender Research. He is the author of What Tech Calls Thinking (2020) and The Cancel Culture Panic (2024), and writes for numerous US and European newspapers and magazines.

This event is cosponsored by the Department of Communication, the Journalism Program, the Michelle R. Clayman Institute for Gender Research, the Stanford Office of Community Engagement, and the Stanford Storytelling Project.

event.description:
What can the Italian lifestyle teach us about living healthy and connected lives? Join our instructor for an engaging webinar as she draws on her experience leading multiple health and wellness programs in Southern Italy. Together, we will explore how Italian food culture, movement, social connection, and centuries-old principles of preventive health can enhance our long-term well-being.

Discover how the traditions of Southern Italy, including the historical Mediterranean lifestyle and the legacy of Salerno, home to Europe's first medical school, the Schola Medica Salernitana, continue to influence modern approaches to nutrition, healthy aging, and disease prevention. Through a combination of lecture and reflection, we will examine how to approach food, physical activity, community, and work-life balance with a refreshed perspective.

A unique aspect of this webinar is its integration of evidence-based nutrition science, historical perspectives on preventive health. This lifestyle approach transcends traditional dieting, calorie counting, and restriction. Instead, it emphasizes sustainable habits that foster both enjoyment and health. You will learn practical strategies for eating mindfully, incorporating movement into your daily routines, building social connections around meals, and cultivating a positive relationship with food.

event.title: PhD Dissertation Defense: Danielle Klinger
event.description:
Title: Non-Destructive Contractility Measurements on Developing Cardioids

Abstract: The force generated by the heart depends in part on how much the cardiac muscle is stretched, and diseases that disrupt this mechanical function, are a major cause of heart failure. Cardioids are 3D engineered heart tissues, derived from human stem cells, that beat spontaneously and reproduce features of the developing heart, making them promising models for studying disease and testing drugs. However, measuring their mechanical function without disrupting the tissue remains challenging. In this work, I developed a non-destructive compression assay to measure contractile force and passive stiffness in intact cardioids. First, I applied it to track individual cardioids throughout maturation and showed that they become smaller, generate more force, and perform more mechanical work with each beat as they mature, similar to the developing human heart. Second, I demonstrated that cardioids exhibit a Frank-Starling response, the increase in contractile force with stretch, that helps the heart adapt to changing demands, and that this response strengthened with maturation. Third, I showed that the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten suppresses this response in a dose-dependent manner. Finally, I applied the assay to a patient-derived model of restrictive cardiomyopathy and found greater contractile force and sensitivity to stretch compared with genetically corrected controls. Together, this work establishes a method for repeatedly measuring the mechanical function of intact human cardiac organoids, enabling studies of cardiac development, drug responses, and disease.

Please contact Anouk Priebe-Garcia for the Zoom link.

event.title: Time Doesn’t Stop: History, Crisis, and the Future of Leftist Political Projects in South America
event.description:
Co-sponsored by the Consulate General of Uruguay in San Francisco

In this lecture, authors Aldo Marchesi y Vania Markarian will present their book El tiempo no para. The book aims to trace the history of the idea of human rights and to understand the impact of that concept on the development of democracies at the close of the 20th century and in progressive governments of the 21st century. It further puts forth questions on the limits of the language of human rights when considering the contemporary crisis. 

Aldo Marchesi holds a PhD in History from New York University and is a Professor in the Department of Theory and Historiography at the Institute for History at The University of the Republic, as well as a member of the Center for Uruguayan Interdisciplinary Studies. Together with colleagues from other disciplines, he recently founded the Institute for Research on Social Justice and Inequality. He is a member of the National System of Researchers in Uruguay. He has served as a visiting professor at universities and research centers in the United States, Chile, Argentina, Colombia, and China. His work has focused on the recent history of Uruguay and the Southern Cone. He has published numerous articles and books. His first book, reissued in 2023, was El Uruguay Inventado: La política audiovisual durante la dictadura. His most recent book, a regional history of the armed Left in the Southern Cone, was published in Spanish and English under the title Hacer la revolución (Making the Revolution). In 2021 he co-authored, with Vania Markarian and Gerardo Caetano, a book on the Left for the collection Historia de los partidos políticos en Uruguay. He has continued researching the Latin American Left in the 20th century and, within a broader context, Uruguay’s recent history. Since 2023, he has co-directed, together with Diego Sempol, a Research Group on the Left. In 2025, he published El tiempo no para: Historia, crisis y futuro para pensar proyectos de izquierda with Vania Markarian. He is currently completing Una historia mínima de las izquierdas latinoamericanas for El Colegio de México. Professor Marchesi has edited and co-edited several volumes and currently serves on the editorial boards of the journals Contemporánea and The Global Sixties. His current research project is Una Historia intellectual y politics de la idea de pobreza en el Uruguay contemporáneo (1943–2010). As part of this project, he was a research member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. This fall, he is a Tinker Visiting Professor at the Teresa Lozano Long Institute of Latin American Studies at the University of Texas at Austin.

Vania Markarian is the Coordinator of the General Archive at the University of the Republic (Udelar), a full-time tenured professor at the same institution, and a member of the National System of Researchers. She holds a PhD in History from Columbia University and a degree in Historical Sciences from Udelar. She has served as a visiting professor and researcher at various universities in Latin America (such as UNGS, UNSAM, and UFMG) and the United States (including Columbia University, the City University of New York, and Princeton University), as well as at the Sorbonne Nouvelle and the École des hautes études en sciences sociales in France. From 2019 to 2021, she served as President of the Uruguayan Association of Historians. She has published books and articles on her areas of expertise both in Uruguay and abroad. Her main works include Idos y recién llegados: La izquierda uruguaya en el exilio y las redes transnacionales de derechos humanos (1967-1984)—originally published by Routledge as Left in Transformation: Uruguayan Exiles and the Latin American Human Rights Networks—and El 68 uruguayo: El movimiento estudiantil entre molotovs y música beat, which was also published in English by the University of California Press. Her most recent book is Universidad, revolución y dólares: Dos estudios sobre la Guerra Fría cultural en el Uruguay de los sesenta (2020). In 2025, she co-authored El tiempo no para: Historia, crisis y utopía para pensar proyectos de izquierda with Aldo Marchesi.

Photo Credit: Magdalena Gutiérrez

event.title: "Looking for cousins": Affective recognition between Black migrants and Afro-Mexicans in Mexico’s "mestizo" state
tags: Latinx and Latin American Literary Studies
event.description:
The Global Studies in Migration and Diaspora Workshop will be hosting Darlène Dubuisson, an Assistant Professor in the Department of African American Studies at the University of California, Berkeley. 

Building upon Deborah Thomas’s “deep affective recognition,” Dubuission considers how Black migrants and AfroMexicans in Mexico desire recognition of their blackness through one another. According to Thomas, “deep affective recognition” represents “an embodied psychic recognition that decimates modernist imperial dualisms” and provides a “basis for new socialities.” How might we understand this desire for recognition among Black migrants and Afro-Mexicans as a form of diasporic longing based on the notion of cousinship, or collateral consanguinity—relatives who have a common ancestry but are not direct descendants? And how might  cousinship represent a new basis for sociality?

event.title: Book Talk - Fear of Queer Taiwan: Anti-LGBTQ Movements between Taiwan and the U.S. Religious Right
event.description: Taiwan has been praised as the first Asian country to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019, celebrating its vibrant democracy and LGBTQ+ communities. Taking a different approach to studying this social change, Dr. Ying-Chao Kao’s new book—Fear of Queer Taiwan: Anti-LGBTQ Movements between Taiwan and the U.S. Religious Right (NYU Press 2026)—focuses on anti-LGBTQ conservatives who fervently opposed marriage equality and LGBTQ+-inclusive education. As a queer Christian, LGBTQ activist, and gender equity educator, Kao conducted 23 months of ethnography in conservative churches and interviewed over 100 people whose political ideologies ranged widely from the far right to the far left. In this talk, Kao will delineate the rise and fall of Taiwanese anti-LGBTQ conservatism, offering a new theoretical framework called “liquid conservatism” to understand the liquidity (mobility, heterogeneity, and transformability) of modern moral conservatism. Particularly, he will reveal the transnational networks through which global conservative groups distribute resources and discourses among “Asian Tigers” (South Korea, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Singapore) and their American, African, and European counterparts. Based on Queer Asian studies, Kao will discuss inter-Asian comparisons of LGBTQ-related attitudes and policies, highlighting Taiwan LGBTQ experiences’ socio-political implications for global Asias and the world.

event.title: CEE PhD Defense - Bryam Xavier Astudillo Carpio, "Assessing practical design methods for strongback braced frames using hazard-consistent collapse risk analysis"
event.description:
Abstract:


Improving community resilience requires structural systems that limit structural damage and reduce downtime after an earthquake. Strongback braced frames (SBFs) with buckling-restrained braces (BRBs) offer an alternative to more traditional braced frames by reducing drift concentrations. Particularly, SBFs use a stiff, essentially elastic vertical truss (i.e., “strongback”) that redistributes seismic demands, enables a more uniform drift distribution, and mitigates story mechanisms. However, challenges in linking practical design methods to collapse performance, while accounting for substantial higher-mode force demands in the strongback, hinder SBF adoption in practice. This dissertation develops design and collapse risk assessment methods able to account for first- and higher-mode demands in SBFs. First, the proposed Multi-Modal Capacity Design (MMCD) method uses free-body diagrams to gain intuition on load paths, providing practical estimates of strongback force demands while accounting for nonlinear behavior in the BRBs and other energy dissipators. Second, the proposed Spectral Hazard Consistency Assessment (SHCA) method measures how well ground-motion records can represent the underlying probabilistic seismic hazard across a range of periods and shaking intensities, supporting more robust SBF collapse risk estimates with reduced dependence on the period used to define seismic demands. Third, the collapse capacity resulting from several design methods with varying levels of modeling complexity was assessed, including Modal Pushover Analysis (MPA) and Multi-R Response Spectrum Analysis (MRRSA), which account for first- and higher-mode force demands using nonlinear and linear elastic models, respectively. Hazard-consistent collapse assessment showed that SBF archetypes with strongbacks designed without accounting for higher-mode force demands result in unacceptably high collapse probabilities, exceeding the target of 1% in 50 years. In contrast, designs using MPA and MRRSA to account for higher-mode force demands meet this collapse risk threshold. Comparisons with FEMA P-695 highlight the influence of spectral shape and ground-motion record selection on assessed collapse performance. Together, these contributions improve understanding of SBF force demands, support hazard-consistent collapse risk assessment of SBF, and demonstrate the importance of accounting for higher modes in practical SBF design, informing future seismic design guidelines and building-code provisions.

event.title: Christopher Ong | Research Acceleration: The View Inside OpenAI
event.description:
In the last year, AI models have rapidly improved on public benchmarks measuring their ability to carry out research tasks autonomously. Such performance suggests that models may be capable of automating parts of the AI R&D process itself, thereby accelerating the pace of AI progress. However, there is still little empirical data on how these new capabilities have changed the research process within the AI labs at the research frontier. This talk will share findings from OpenAI's recent report on AI-powered research acceleration, which aims to help fill this gap. We will also discuss future research directions for the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI).

The report documents several stylized facts. First, models are increasingly capable of autonomously completing research tasks that would take a human researcher several hours or even days to finish. However, completing longer tasks remains challenging and more frequently requires human intervention. Second, agentic use is rapidly increasing, such that total hours worked by the agent workforce is several times that of the human workforce. Finally, researchers intensely use agents for execution-oriented tasks such as writing code, reviewing technical work, and managing training runs, but high-level planning remains primarily bottlenecked on humans.

event.title: Healthy Holiday Side Dishes
event.description:
Holiday side dishes can be every bit as memorable as the main course. In this virtual cooking demonstration, learn how to prepare colorful, flavor-forward sides that bring seasonal ingredients, satisfying textures, and nourishing foods to the holiday table.

We will share practical ways to make traditional holiday meals feel fresher and more balanced, without sacrificing the comforting flavors people look forward to all year. You will learn how to use vegetables, whole grains, legumes, herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, and healthy fats to create dishes that support overall well-being.

The class will also cover make-ahead strategies, ingredient substitutions, and simple ways to accommodate a variety of dietary needs and preferences. By the end of the session, you will have versatile recipes and ideas you can use for holiday gatherings, winter meals, and seasonal entertaining.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants.

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.

Request disability accommodations and access info.

event.title: How the World Learns: Education & Culture from Five Countries.
event.description:
As part of International Education Week, join us for a panel discussion that brings together five speakers from around the world to talk about education and culture.

Each speaker will share their own experience of education in their home country. Then we will open the floor for discussion and your questions.

The conversation will explore:

  • Access, cost, and support: who can get an education, what is free, and what help is available
  • Culture: how values and ideas of success show up in education
  • Comparison: how education systems differ, including from the US
  • AI and change: how technology is reshaping learning, and whether it makes education fairer

Come curious and bring your questions.

Moderator:
Aidana Jussupova, moderator and speaker for Kazakhstan, active Ambassador of the Stanford International Spouse Community.

event.title: Pediatric Orthopedics and Sports Medicine Lecture Series: Pediatric Lower Extremity Alignment and In-Toeing
event.description:
Overview

This lecture will provide an overview of pediatric lower extremity development, helping learners distinguish physiologic variations from pathologic findings. Learners will review common causes of in-toeing gait, develop strategies for identifying the source of rotational deformities through physical examination, and recognize red flags in gait and lower extremity alignment. The session will also provide practical guidance for counseling families about expected natural history and determining when further intervention is warranted.

Registration

Registration is required.

All practitioners: free.

Credits

AMA PRA Category 1 Credits™ (1.00 hours), BOC Category A Hours/CEUs (1.00 hours), Non-Physician Participation Credit (1.00 hours), Occupational Therapy Contact Hours (1.00 hours), Physical Therapy Contact Hours (1.00 hours)

Target Audience
Specialties - Orthopedics & Sports Medicine, Pediatrics
Professions - Athletic Trainer, Fellow/Resident, Non-Physician, Occupational Therapist, Physical Therapist
 
Objectives
At the conclusion of this activity, learners should be able to:


1. Review pediatric lower extremity alignment and differentiate physiologic from pathologic. 
2. Discuss the most common causes of in-toeing gait in children and identify the source of rotational deformity through physical exam. 
3. Identify red flags in gait and lower extremity alignment. 
4. Counsel families on natural history and indications for further intervention.
